# Flourishing Business Canvas Analysis: Dawetrest Green Hatchery (Draž, Croatia)

## Goals

The **Dawetrest Green Hatchery** initiative pursues multiple intertwined goals centered on ecological, social, and economic sustainability. The primary mission is to **restore and enhance the floodplain ecosystem** of the Topoljski Dunavac (a Danube river oxbow in Draž) by breeding and reintroducing native fish species[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}. Key goals include:

-   

-   

    **Biodiversity Restoration:** Rebuild populations of **autochthonous cyprinid fish** (native carp and related species) to enrich aquatic biodiversity and improve the ecological balance of the Danube floodplain[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources"}. This contributes to healthier food webs and habitats for other wildlife.

-   

-   

    **Wetland Bird Support:** Increase food availability for **vulnerable wetland birds** (herons, storks, ibises) by boosting fish stocks. Starting in 2025, the hatchery will release \~**1,200 kg of native fish biomass annually** (in two batches), which is expected to significantly improve the feeding grounds for endangered bird species[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}.

-   

-   

    **Eco-Tourism and Recreation:** Develop **sustainable nature tourism** (sport fishing, bird watching, educational tours) as a complementary activity. By leveraging the improved ecosystem, the project aims to attract visitors for recreational fishing and nature observation, thereby raising awareness and generating local income.

-   

-   

    **Community Livelihoods and Education:** Provide local **socio-economic benefits** such as employment opportunities at the hatchery and tourism services, and engage the community through environmental education programs. The hatchery will serve as a learning site to demonstrate sustainable aquaculture and conservation practices to students, visitors, and other stakeholders.

-   

-   

    **Innovation and Replicability:** Serve as a **demonstration model** for sustainable wetland restoration that can be replicated in other regions. As part of the broader EU-funded DaWetRest project, this initiative seeks to prove the feasibility and scalability of nature-based solutions for wetland ecosystems[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Kao%20strate%C5%A1ki%20partneri%2C%20ove%20%C4%87e,%C5%A1irenju%20aktivnosti%20obnove%20slatkovodnih%20ekosustava){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Kao%20strate%C5%A1ki%20partneri%2C%20ove%20%C4%87e,%C5%A1irenju%20aktivnosti%20obnove%20slatkovodnih%20ekosustava"}. A long-term goal is to share knowledge and **enable other Danube Basin communities** to implement similar hatchery-based restoration measures, amplifying the impact beyond Draž.

-   

These goals align with international conservation objectives and EU Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters,” marrying ecological regeneration with community development. By achieving these goals, the Dawetrest Green Hatchery hopes to **sustain flourishing for people and nature** in Baranja and serve as a beacon for integrated conservation enterprise.

## Benefits

**Benefits** refer to the positive outcomes and value generated by the hatchery initiative for various stakeholders and the system as a whole. The project’s benefits span environmental gains, social improvements, and economic value:

-   

-   

    **Environmental Benefits:** The primary benefit is a **healthier aquatic ecosystem** in the Topoljski Dunavac. Increased native fish populations will contribute to improved water quality and ecological stability (as fish help control algae and support nutrient cycles). The boosted fish biomass provides a richer food source for predatory birds and other wildlife, thereby enhancing overall **biodiversity**[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}. In the long term, a thriving wetland ecosystem can offer improved ecosystem services such as natural water filtration and floodplain resilience.

-   

-   

    **Social Benefits:** The initiative fosters **community well-being and pride** in local natural heritage. It creates opportunities for environmental education (school visits, volunteer events for fish release) and community engagement in conservation. Local residents benefit from new recreational opportunities (e.g. family-friendly fishing events, nature walks) and from the preservation of cultural traditions related to the Danube wetlands and fishing. The project also contributes to **public health and enjoyment** by protecting a clean, natural environment for people to enjoy.

-   

-   

    **Economic Benefits:** While primarily conservation-focused, the hatchery yields economic value through **eco-tourism and related activities**. Sport fishermen and nature tourists drawn to the area bring revenue to local guides, accommodations, and restaurants. The hatchery itself may create a few direct jobs (facility managers, aquaculture technicians, tour guides) and support indirect jobs in the hospitality sector. In addition, the project’s existence (with EU funding and future grants) injects investment into the region’s rural economy. Over time, if fish stocks become abundant, there could be **sustainable fishing yields** for local fishing communities (e.g. regulated harvests or permit fees), aligning conservation with economic use.

-   

-   

    **Institutional and Knowledge Benefits:** For the project partners and broader scientific community, the hatchery generates valuable **data and know-how**. Successful breeding of native species and monitoring results contribute to research on wetland restoration. The site functions as a **living lab** where innovative techniques (e.g. low-impact aquaculture, monitoring systems) can be tested and demonstrated. These insights benefit policy-makers and other regions by providing a proof-of-concept that strong environmental outcomes can coincide with social and economic value creation.

-   

In summary, the Dawetrest Green Hatchery co-creates a win-win scenario: revitalizing nature while benefiting people. The **triple bottom line** outcomes (environmental, social, financial) strengthen the case for continuing and scaling such initiatives.

## Costs

This section outlines the **cost structure** and sacrifices associated with the hatchery initiative. Like any enterprise, the project incurs financial costs, but it also must account for operational challenges and any trade-offs:

-   

-   

    **Capital Expenditure:** Significant upfront **investment costs** were required to establish the hatchery. Construction of the facility (renovating or building tanks, ponds, and a small hatchery building) and procurement of specialized equipment (pumps, aeration blowers, filtration units, backup generators, a GSM-alarm system for emergencies, etc.) demanded capital. Much of this was funded by the EU’s DaWetRest project grant, offsetting direct local spending. However, any cost overruns or future expansions would need additional financing.

-   

-   

    **Operating Costs:** The hatchery bears ongoing **operational expenses**. These include energy costs for running water pumps and aerators continuously (electricity consumption is a major cost driver), fish feed and hatchery supplies, water monitoring chemicals or lab tests, and maintenance of equipment and infrastructure. Staff salaries or stipends for the hatchery managers/technicians form an essential part of the cost structure. There are also costs for logistics – e.g. fuel and vehicle use to transport fish during release events, and procurement of fingerling containers or oxygen for transport. Additionally, running eco-tourism (if offering tours or events) involves marketing costs and costs of hospitality (safety gear, fishing gear maintenance, etc.).

-   

-   

    **Administrative and Compliance Costs:** Ensuring all necessary **permits and regulatory compliance** has both financial and time costs. The project had to obtain environmental permits, water usage rights, and building permissions aligned with Croatian law and EU conservation regulations. Regular reporting to funders (EU) and monitoring agencies requires staff time and resources. Insurance for the facility (liability, asset insurance) is another cost.

-   

-   

    **Opportunity Costs:** Dedicating part of the land and water resources to a conservation hatchery means those resources are not used for other purposes (e.g., commercial fish farming or agriculture). While the long-term benefits outweigh this, it’s a trade-off to consider in the cost structure.

-   

-   

    **Future Financial Sustainability:** After the grant period, the hatchery will need a **sustainable funding model**. If revenue from eco-tourism or local government support does not cover operating costs, additional funds (grants, sponsorships, or cross-subsidies) will be needed. This represents a potential financial risk/cost if not managed – essentially the cost of securing long-term financing (which could include dedicating staff time to fundraising or proposal writing).

-   

Overall, the initiative’s costs are justified by its benefits, but prudent financial planning is required. By carefully managing energy and feed efficiency, leveraging volunteer help for certain activities, and integrating tourism revenue, the hatchery aims to keep recurrent costs manageable. Importantly, some **environmental costs** (e.g. carbon footprint of energy use) are mitigated by design, as discussed under Value Co-destructions.

## Ecosystem Actors

*Ecosystem Context:* *The Dawetrest Green Hatchery is embedded in the Topoljski Dunavac wetlands (pictured above, with the hatchery tanks in the foreground and the floodplain water body and riparian greenery beyond). This setting highlights the diverse ecosystem actors – human and non-human – connected by the project.*

The **ecosystem actors** encompass all entities (people, organisms, and institutions) in the hatchery’s surrounding environment who affect or are affected by the enterprise. These include both **human actors** (stakeholders and broader community members) and **non-human actors** (wildlife, ecological features) that have a stake in the ecosystem’s health:

-   

-   

    **Aquatic Ecosystem & Wildlife:** At the core is the **Topoljski Dunavac** side-channel ecosystem itself – its water, sediments, and ecological processes. Native **fish species** (e.g. wild carp, tench, pike-perch, and other cyprinids) are key actors, as the hatchery exists for their propagation. Also crucial are the **wetland birds** (heron, stork, ibis families) and other fauna (amphibians, aquatic invertebrates) that rely on the fish and wetland for food and habitat. Even the **vegetation** (water plants, reed beds, riparian forests) is an actor, as it provides habitat structure and water quality regulation. These non-human actors have “needs” to survive and flourish (food, habitat, clean water), which the project aims to support.

-   

-   

    **Local Community:** The people living in Draž and surrounding Baranja villages constitute another actor group. They include local **residents and landowners** (some may live adjacent to the wetland or use it traditionally), as well as **local fishermen** who have cultural and livelihood ties to these waters. The community’s well-being is intertwined with the health of the environment and the opportunities the project creates.

-   

-   

    **Visitors and Tourists:** **Nature enthusiasts, anglers, and eco-tourists** who come (or will come) to the area form an important set of actors. They seek recreational and educational experiences. Their presence and behavior can impact the ecosystem (positively, through citizen science or funding conservation, or negatively if not managed). They are potential customers whose satisfaction and support are important for the project’s success.

-   

-   

    **Project Implementers and Partners:** This group includes the **project team and partner organizations**. The Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and Naval Architecture (FSB) and the Adriatic Innovation Center are key actors who designed and launched the hatchery[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}. The **Odra Angling Association** (a sport-fishing NGO) and local fisheries organizations in Osijek-Baranja are deeply involved[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"} – their members may volunteer, contribute expertise, and assist in fish releases. Also part of this sphere are **scientists and engineers** who have a stake in the project’s research outcomes.

-   

-   

    **Governance and Regulatory Actors:** Local and regional authorities (e.g. **Municipality of Draž**, **Osijek-Baranja County**, **Croatian Water Management – Hrvatske Vode**, and the **Nature Park Kopački Rit** administration) are actors who shape the context via regulations, permits, and support. National bodies (Ministry of Environment or Agriculture) and EU bodies (the EU Mission program officers) also play a role as actors providing oversight, funding, and policy context. They are concerned with the project meeting regulatory standards and broader environmental objectives.

-   

-   

    **Extended Ecosystem (Network) Actors:** Beyond the immediate locality, the hatchery is connected to a network of **Danube region stakeholders**. Other DEMO sites in the DaWetRest project, associated regions looking to replicate the approach, and international conservation organizations (e.g. WWF Danube-Carpathian Programme, wetland restoration networks) are actors who interact indirectly. They watch the project’s progress, potentially exchange knowledge, and have an interest in its success or lessons learned.

-   

By recognizing this full spectrum of ecosystem actors, the hatchery’s strategy can be attuned to the interdependencies between people, planet, and the project’s operations. In the next sections, we delve into the needs and engagements of these actors, and how value is co-created among them.

## Needs

The **Needs** block identifies the fundamental needs, interests, or problems of the ecosystem actors that the Dawetrest Green Hatchery must consider. Understanding these needs ensures the initiative creates relevant value. Key needs include:

-   

-   

    **Ecological Needs:** The **wetland ecosystem** needs restoration to a healthier state. This includes the need for *repopulation of native fish* (to fill an ecological niche and stabilize food webs) and *habitat quality improvement* (clean, oxygen-rich water and suitable spawning grounds). The **fish species** themselves need sufficient food, appropriate water conditions, and safe breeding habitats – conditions that have been degraded in past decades. The **wetland birds** need an abundant food supply (fish and aquatic life) and undisturbed nesting areas. Overall, the ecosystem needs interventions that reverse biodiversity loss and improve resilience.

-   

-   

    **Community Needs:** The **local community** needs sustainable development opportunities. Many rural communities in Baranja face economic challenges; thus there is a need for *local jobs* and *income sources* that do not degrade the environment. The community also needs *flood protection* and *water management* (healthy floodplain wetlands can help buffer floods and improve groundwater). Culturally, locals need to maintain their *connection to the land and water* – they value the Danube heritage and have a need to see it preserved. There may also be a need for *youth engagement* to counter rural out-migration – projects like this can inspire younger generations to stay or return.

-   

-   

    **Visitor Needs:** **Tourists and anglers** need an enjoyable and authentic experience. Anglers specifically need *healthy fish populations* to have successful catches (especially if sport fishing is a draw). Nature tourists need *rich wildlife sightings* (birds, scenic landscapes) and *educational information* to appreciate the site. All visitors need the area to be accessible and safe (basic infrastructure like trails, signage, perhaps viewing platforms or fishing piers). They also expect the site to be well-managed so that their activities are sustainable and the natural beauty is maintained for future visits.

-   

-   

    **Partner and Organizational Needs:** The **project partners** and implementing team have needs related to successfully running the hatchery. They need *adequate funding and resources* to operate (addressed through the EU grant and hopefully future revenues). They require *technical knowledge and skilled personnel* to breed fish and maintain equipment. Partners like FSB (university) need *research data and innovation outcomes* – the project should yield insights or technologies (e.g., a low-energy hatchery design) that justify their involvement. Local NGOs (fishing clubs) need *collaboration and influence* in the project to ensure it aligns with on-the-ground realities; their need is to see fish stocks and fisheries improve in line with their conservation goals.

-   

-   

    **Regulatory and Societal Needs:** Authorities and society at large have a need to meet **conservation and climate targets**. There’s pressure to restore ecosystems under EU directives and the Mission program – hence the need for *effective restoration solutions*. Regulators need the project to maintain *compliance* with laws (no invasive species, no pollution) and to *demonstrate impact* (through monitoring). More broadly, society needs successful examples of businesses that integrate environmental and social value; the need is for *models of sustainability* that can be learned from to address global challenges.

-   

By addressing these diverse needs, the hatchery can ensure it remains relevant and supported. The design of its services (fish production, tourism experiences, education) explicitly aims to meet these needs: feeding the ecosystem, revitalizing community livelihoods, satisfying visitor curiosity, and fulfilling conservation mandates.

## Stakeholders

**Stakeholders** are the actors who actively participate in or are directly affected by the enterprise’s value exchanges. They have a stake in the success of the hatchery and often contribute resources or receive benefits from it. The Dawetrest Green Hatchery’s key stakeholders include:

-   

-   

    **Project Consortium & Core Team:** This includes the **DaWetRest project partners** who established and run the hatchery. The Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and Naval Architecture (FSB) at University of Zagreb is a stakeholder providing technical leadership (designing the recirculation system, monitoring tech, etc.). The **Adriatic Innovation Center** and the **Odra Angling Association** are also core stakeholders that helped launch the Green Hatchery[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}. They share in decision-making and bring expertise (innovation in sustainable aquaculture, and practical fisheries knowledge respectively). These stakeholders are invested in achieving the project outcomes and proving the concept.

-   

-   

    **Local Fisheries NGOs and Associations:** Regional groups such as county-level **sports fishing clubs and fisheries associations** are stakeholders deeply involved in implementation. For example, local NGOs in Osijek-Baranja responsible for fisheries are collaborating to release the hatchery-reared fish[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}. These stakeholders contribute volunteer labor, traditional knowledge, and help ensure the project aligns with local conservation efforts. In return, they gain improved fish stocks and possibly a role in managing the resource (co-management).

-   

-   

    **Municipality and Government Agencies:** The **Municipality of Draž** and relevant county agencies are stakeholders because they likely provided permits, possibly land or infrastructure support, and have an interest in the project’s success (as it benefits the local economy and environment). **Hrvatske Vode** (Croatian Waters), the national water management authority, is a stakeholder given their mandate to manage water bodies – they are involved in or informed about the restoration of the Dunavac channel and the hatchery’s water use. The **Kopački Rit Nature Park Authority** is another stakeholder, as Topoljski Dunavac is hydrologically connected to the larger protected wetlands; park managers would coordinate on biodiversity goals and ensure the project supports the park’s conservation objectives. National ministries (Environment, Agriculture) and EU Mission representatives, while not on-site, are key stakeholders in terms of oversight and broader impact – their stake is largely in seeing policy goals met and funds well-spent.

-   

-   

    **Local Community Members:** The people living in the vicinity (Draž and nearby settlements) are stakeholders who may experience direct impacts. Some individuals might be employed by the project (thus **employees** are stakeholders), or supply services (e.g. a local contractor maintaining the facility, or local farmers providing grain for fish feed). **Residents** have a stake in how the project affects their environment (e.g. improved water quality, or any changes in land use). They also stand to benefit from increased tourism. Their support or opposition can influence the project’s success, making them de facto stakeholders who need to be kept informed and involved.

-   

-   

    **Eco-Tourists and Anglers (Customers):** **Visitors** who come for sport fishing or nature tourism are a type of stakeholder – essentially the customers of the services offered. They exchange money (or at least time/attention) for the experience provided by the hatchery’s existence (catching fish, touring the facility, etc.). Their satisfaction influences word-of-mouth and future demand. Responsible anglers could also become partners in conservation (for instance, through catch-and-release practices or citizen science reporting of fish tags), blurring the line between customer and partner stakeholder.

-   

-   

    **The Ecosystem Itself:** In a flourishing business model perspective, even the **non-human environment can be considered a stakeholder** – often represented by proxies. For instance, the **fish populations and wetland habitat** have a stake in the enterprise because its operations directly determine their fate. While they cannot speak for themselves, their “stake” is represented by conservation scientists or NGOs. This project essentially treats the ecosystem as a primary stakeholder by orienting its entire value proposition around ecological well-being.

-   

Each of these stakeholders has specific expectations and contributions. The hatchery’s governance (next section) is designed to balance their interests. By engaging stakeholders from scientific experts to local citizens and even the ecosystem, the initiative builds a coalition that underpins its long-term resilience.

## Relationships

The **relationships** block describes how the Green Hatchery engages and interacts with its stakeholders to maintain their support, satisfaction, and active participation. Given the diverse stakeholder groups, the initiative employs a variety of relationship strategies:

-   

-   

    **Co-Creation & Collaboration:** A defining relationship approach is treating partners and community members as **co-creators** of the project. For example, the project team works closely with **local fishing NGOs** in planning and executing fish releases[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}. Regular coordination meetings, joint training sessions, and shared responsibilities (like co-hosting events) ensure these partners feel ownership. This collaborative relationship builds trust and aligns everyone on common goals (restoring fish and birds).

-   

-   

    **Community Engagement:** With local residents, the project emphasizes **transparency and inclusion**. Public meetings (e.g., at the Draž municipal hall) were held during project planning[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Prezentacija%20Koncepcijskog%20rje%C5%A1enja%20restauracije%20Lorencovog,dunavca){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Prezentacija%20Koncepcijskog%20rje%C5%A1enja%20restauracije%20Lorencovog,dunavca"}[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=U%20rujnu%202023,%C4%8Dlanovi%20projektnog%20tima%20Hrvatskih%20voda){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=U%20rujnu%202023,%C4%8Dlanovi%20projektnog%20tima%20Hrvatskih%20voda"} to present plans (like the restoration of a nearby side-arm) and gather input. This open dialogue helps maintain a positive relationship with the community. Ongoing, the hatchery may host open-house days or volunteer opportunities (such as community fish release days or wetland clean-up events), turning local people into active supporters. By demonstrating tangible benefits (like better fishing or tourism income) and soliciting feedback, the project nurtures goodwill and local pride.

-   

-   

    **Customer Experience & Education:** For **visitors and tourists**, the relationship is managed by providing a **high-quality, educational experience**. Trained guides or staff engage with visitors, offering tours of the hatchery facility, explaining the aquaculture process, and highlighting the ecological importance of the site. Sport fishers are engaged through a permit or reservation system that may include briefings on rules (catch-and-release, allowed areas) to ensure sustainable enjoyment. Maintaining an active online presence (via a website or social media updates under the DaWetRest umbrella) is also key – sharing success stories (e.g., bird sightings, fish growth updates) keeps potential visitors interested and informed.

-   

-   

    **Governance and Reporting:** With government bodies and funders, the relationship is formal and accountability-oriented. The project team provides **regular reports and data** demonstrating progress toward goals (e.g., monitoring results of fish survival and bird populations). By maintaining a record of compliance and success, they strengthen the relationship with regulators and sponsors. There is also a feedback loop: the team consults with park authorities and water managers to align hatchery operations with broader conservation plans (e.g., adjusting fish release timing to fit natural flood cycles or park guidelines). This cooperative relationship with authorities ensures ongoing support and the smooth issuance of permits in future.

-   

-   

    **Knowledge Network Relationships:** As a demonstration project, the hatchery cultivates relationships in a **wider knowledge network**. This includes collaborations with researchers (sharing data for scientific studies, hosting student projects or thesis work on-site) and exchanges with other wetland restoration projects. For instance, the team likely interacts with other **DaWetRest DEMO sites** and associated regions, providing updates and lessons learned. These relationships are maintained through workshops, conferences, and digital platforms, positioning the hatchery as a valued node in a learning community. Such relationships not only enhance the project’s credibility but also attract new ideas and potentially new funding or partners.

-   

In all these relationships, the tone is one of **partnership, mutual benefit, and stewardship**. By actively managing relationships—be it through community meetings, visitor outreach, or transparent governance—the Green Hatchery ensures continued stakeholder buy-in and adapts to their needs over time.

## Channels

**Channels** describe the pathways through which the Green Hatchery delivers its value propositions to stakeholders and how it reaches and communicates with them. The initiative uses a mix of physical and informational channels:

-   

-   

    **Fish Release Channels:** To deliver the **conservation value (fish populations) to the ecosystem**, the project uses planned **biannual stocking events** as the channel. Hatchery-raised juvenile or adult fish are transported (via aerated tank trucks or containers) to strategic release points along the Topoljski Dunavac. This logistical channel is carefully managed to minimize stress to fish – timing releases in spring and fall when conditions are optimal. In essence, these events are the “distribution channel” for the core product (live fish) to the wild ecosystem. They are often done in collaboration with local NGOs and could double as public events, thereby also serving as community outreach channels (educating participants and media about the restoration).

-   

-   

    **Eco-Tourism & Recreation Channels:** To reach **tourists and anglers**, the project leverages **tourism networks and media**. This includes online channels: a project or municipal tourism website listing the Green Hatchery as a point of interest, social media pages showcasing the wetland wildlife, and possibly features on travel blogs or local news. Regionally, the initiative works with the **Baranja Tourist Board** and nature park visitor centers (like Kopački Rit’s info center) to direct interested visitors to Draž. Physical signage is another channel – for instance, signage on nearby roads pointing to the hatchery or interpretive panels at the site explaining the project. For anglers, channels might involve local fishing shops or angling forums where news about improved fishing spots is shared, as well as a permit system (perhaps available at a municipal office or online) that channels anglers to the site in a controlled manner.

-   

-   

    **Educational Outreach Channels:** The hatchery uses **educational channels** to deliver knowledge to students, researchers, and the public. This includes organizing school field trips (in coordination with local schools and universities), where students visit the hatchery and learn about wetland ecology – the “channel” here is direct on-site engagement facilitated by teachers and hatchery staff. Another channel is workshops or open seminars, possibly hosted at the community center or even virtually, where experts share findings (for example, presenting monitoring results to interested citizens or academics). Printed brochures or info booklets available at municipal offices or tourist info points serve as take-home channels to spread awareness about the project’s purpose and results.

-   

-   

    **Communications and Media:** Given the demonstrative nature of the project, communication channels are very important. The project team likely produces **regular newsletters or press releases** (often through the DaWetRest consortium communications) that highlight milestones like the hatchery opening, first release, notable species observed, etc. These are disseminated via email lists, the consortium’s website, and media outlets (press, environmental magazines). Local radio or TV may occasionally cover major events (like the opening ceremony or an annual “Wetland Day” celebration on-site), serving as mass communication channels to the broader public. Such media coverage helps rally support and recognition beyond the immediate stakeholder circle.

-   

-   

    **Feedback and Interaction Channels:** Channels are not one-way; the project also has means for stakeholders to reach back or interact. For instance, a **visitor feedback system** (guestbook at the site or online reviews) is a channel for receiving input on the eco-tourism experience. Community members can voice concerns or suggestions through public forums or a dedicated contact person (perhaps a liaison employed by the project or municipality). The project’s presence in local governance meetings or environmental committees also acts as a channel for ongoing dialogue.

-   

By utilizing these diverse channels, the Green Hatchery ensures its value – whether tangible fish or intangible education – effectively reaches its intended beneficiaries. A multi-channel approach also strengthens resilience; if one channel is weak (e.g., fewer tourists in a season), other channels (like community programs or online engagement) keep value flowing and awareness high.

## Products/Services

The **products and services** offered by the Dawetrest Green Hatchery are multifaceted, reflecting its dual role as a conservation initiative and a community enterprise. The key offerings include:

-   

-   

    **Native Fish Stock for Ecosystem Restoration:** The core “product” is the **breeding and supply of native fish** (e.g., common carp, tench, and other indigenous Danube species). Unlike a commercial fish farm that sells fish for consumption, this hatchery’s product is **juvenile and adult fish for release** into the wild. These fish are bred and raised to a hardy stage on-site, specifically to repopulate the Topoljski Dunavac and nearby waters. This service is provided to the ecosystem and indirectly to stakeholders like conservation agencies and local fisheries managers. (If needed, excess juveniles might also be provided to restock other water bodies in the region, extending the service beyond the immediate site.)

-   

-   

    **Sport Fishing Experience:** Capitalizing on improved fish populations, the project offers **regulated sport fishing** opportunities. This can be seen as a service to recreational anglers – a form of eco-tourism product. For example, catch-and-release fishing days might be organized, where anglers can fish in designated stretches of the Dunavac known to be stocked. They pay for permits or tours, and in return get a quality fishing experience (with a good chance of catching native species in a natural setting) guided by sustainable principles. This service is carefully managed to avoid overfishing; it’s as much about the experience as the catch, often emphasizing education on species and conservation.

-   

-   

    **Nature Tourism and Guided Tours:** For non-anglers, the hatchery provides **nature tourism services**. This may include *guided tours of the hatchery facility* itself – visitors can see the breeding tanks, learn about aquaculture technology, and perhaps observe juvenile fish rearing. Additionally, guides may take visitors on *nature walks* around the wetland, highlighting birdwatching spots and explaining the ecological restoration underway. There could be a small visitor center or interpretive trail as part of this service, offering informational displays. These tourism services cater to families, school groups, and eco-tourists, offering them an educational recreation activity.

-   

-   

    **Environmental Education Programs:** The hatchery functions as an **outdoor classroom**. It offers programs such as workshops for local farmers or fishermen on sustainable practices, school educational programs aligned with biology curricula, and volunteer citizen science opportunities (e.g., counting birds or helping with habitat clean-up). These services might not generate revenue directly, but they fulfill the project’s educational mission. In some cases, funding for such programs might come from partnerships or grants (for example, a workshop sponsored by a conservation NGO or government agency).

-   

-   

    **Research and Consulting Services:** Given the innovative nature of the Green Hatchery, it can offer **expertise as a service**. Project experts might provide consulting to other regions or groups interested in replicating the model (sharing guidelines on building a “green hatchery”, designing monitoring plans, etc.). The facility can also host **research projects** – for instance, scientists might pay (or collaborate) to use the site for experiments on fish behavior or water quality improvement techniques. Over time, this could formalize into a service where the hatchery is a recognized demonstration site that offers training sessions or seminars for professionals (e.g., training other wetland park managers or aquaculture specialists in nature-based solutions).

-   

-   

    **Fish and Aquaculture Products (Potential):** In the future, the hatchery could produce **limited commercial outputs** to support its finances, as long as it doesn’t conflict with conservation. For example, it might grow some fingerlings or ornamental native fish for sale to local pond owners or conservation bodies in other regions. It could also pilot the cultivation of native **fish for local cuisine** on a small scale, partnering with local restaurants to feature a “Danube native fish” dish – thereby raising awareness through gastronomy. These ideas would be carefully balanced against the primary aim of ecosystem restoration, but they represent possible service extensions that **co-create value with the local economy**.

-   

By offering this suite of products and services, the Dawetrest Green Hatchery not only advances its ecological goals but also creates tangible experiences and outputs that engage people. Each offering is designed to reinforce the others (for instance, tourists pay for tours that support the breeding program; the thriving ecosystem draws more tourists, and so on), creating a synergistic business model for sustainability.

## Value Co-Creations

**Value co-creation** refers to the positive value jointly created by the enterprise and its stakeholders – the mutual benefits and improvements that result from their interactions. The Dawetrest Green Hatchery generates numerous co-created values across environmental, social, and economic dimensions:

-   

-   

    **Ecological Value (Environment & Enterprise):** A flourishing wetland ecosystem is a prime co-creation of value between the hatchery and nature. The enterprise provides fish and active stewardship, while the environment responds with improved biodiversity and ecosystem health. This yields value for the enterprise (success in its mission) and value for nature (recovery and resilience). For example, as the hatchery reintroduces native fish, **the ecosystem co-creates a balanced food web**, resulting in cleaner water and robust fish populations that sustain themselves – a positive feedback loop beneficial to both the project (which can scale back intensive breeding over time) and the environment.

-   

-   

    **Food Web Support (Wildlife & Community):** By boosting fish numbers, the hatchery and the wetland together co-create **abundant food resources** for predators like herons and storks[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}. The value here is healthier bird populations and potentially higher breeding success for endangered species. This is co-created by the project (providing fish) and the birds/wetland (utilizing that food to thrive). In turn, the community gains value in the form of **natural heritage preservation** – iconic bird species remain part of the local landscape for future generations to enjoy.

-   

-   

    **Knowledge and Innovation (Enterprise & Academia):** The collaboration with research partners co-creates new **scientific knowledge and technical innovation**. The hatchery provides a testbed and data; academic stakeholders provide analysis and expertise. Together they develop, for instance, more efficient low-energy pumping systems or better methods for raising sensitive species. This co-created knowledge is a valuable output that can be published or used elsewhere, benefiting the enterprise (through improved operations and reputation) and the academic partners (through papers and real-world impact).

-   

-   

    **Economic and Recreational Value (Community & Tourists):** The project co-creates **economic opportunities and recreation** by inviting tourists and anglers into the fold. Tourists get the value of a memorable experience (fishing or wildlife watching in a pristine environment), while their participation (and spending) co-generates income for local guides, B&Bs, and the enterprise’s upkeep. For instance, a guided fishing tour co-creates value: the angler enjoys a catch, the guide earns a living, and the fish (if released) continue to live – an ongoing value for the ecosystem. The community at large sees incremental growth in eco-tourism, diversifying the rural economy.

-   

-   

    **Social Capital and Partnerships (Enterprise & Local Stakeholders):** Through its inclusive approach, the hatchery and its stakeholders co-create **social value** in the form of stronger networks and stewardship ethics. The partnerships with local NGOs and authorities mean that knowledge, responsibility, and credit are shared. This co-created social capital manifests as, say, a local youth group getting involved in nature monitoring – they gain skills and pride (value to them), and the enterprise gains enthusiastic ambassadors and helpers (value to the project). Similarly, cooperation between cross-border or regional stakeholders in the Danube network builds a **community of practice**, co-created by the project’s existence, that can tackle other environmental challenges collectively.

-   

-   

    **Cultural and Educational Value:** The initiative co-creates an **educational legacy** by reviving cultural connections to the wetland. Local elders might share traditional knowledge of fishing or floodplain management with project staff, blending modern science with cultural heritage – a value for both sides. Schoolchildren participating in hatchery visits co-create value: they contribute their curiosity and energy, and in return gain knowledge and inspiration to become future conservationists. This cultural continuity and heightened environmental awareness in society is a subtle but important co-created value emerging from the project.

-   

In all these ways, the hatchery is not just delivering one-way value; it actively **engages stakeholders to co-produce outcomes** that none could achieve alone. The result is a set of benefits that are richer and more sustainable because they are jointly created and owned.

## Value Co-Destructions

Despite its positive aims, the project must be mindful of **value co-destruction**, i.e. any negative value or harm that could be unintentionally co-generated through interactions. Identifying these risks allows for mitigation. Some potential co-destructions include:

-   

-   

    **Environmental Risks:** If not managed properly, the hatchery operations could co-destroy value for the ecosystem. For example, **disease transfer** is a risk – captive-reared fish might introduce pathogens to wild populations, harming the very species we aim to save. This would be a co-destruction by the enterprise (via fish releases) affecting nature. To mitigate this, strict biosecurity and health screening of fish are necessary. Another risk is **genetic impact**: if hatchery fish are not genetically diverse or are selectively bred, their introduction could reduce the genetic fitness of wild stocks. The project must ensure it sources broad genetic stock and perhaps rotate breeding fish to avoid inbreeding. Additionally, any effluent or wastewater from the tanks, if released, could pollute local water; however, the design presumably recirculates or treats water, minimizing this co-destruction.

-   

-   

    **Disturbance to Wildlife:** Eco-tourism activities, if unchecked, could inadvertently co-destroy value for wildlife. Increased human presence (boats, anglers, photographers) might disturb nesting birds or other sensitive species. Noise, trampling of vegetation, or litter from visitors would degrade the habitat. This is a co-destruction between tourists (enjoying recreation) and the ecosystem (suffering disturbance). The project mitigates this by enforcing guidelines: e.g., limiting visitor numbers in breeding season, creating observation distances for birdwatching, and educating visitors to carry out trash. Careful zoning (separating a core conservation zone from a tourism zone) can allow enjoyment without destruction.

-   

-   

    **Social Tensions or Inequity:** There is a possibility of co-destroyed social value if certain stakeholders feel excluded or if benefits are not fairly distributed. For instance, if most tourism benefits go to outsiders or a few individuals, local residents might feel resentment, which erodes community cohesion. Also, local fishermen might worry that new rules (like catch-and-release or protected areas) limit their traditional practices – a perceived loss of value for them. The enterprise and community together might inadvertently create social conflict if communication falters. Proactively, the project seeks to avoid this by involving local stakeholders in decisions (so they co-own the rules) and ensuring any new income streams have local participation (thus sharing value to prevent envy or conflict).

-   

-   

    **Economic Viability Challenges:** A subtle form of co-destruction is if the project’s financial sustainability falters – this could destroy value for multiple stakeholders. For example, if tourist numbers don’t meet expectations, the revenue shortfall combined with high operating costs could lead to cutbacks or closure of the hatchery, wasting the initial investments and dashing community hopes. This negative outcome would be co-created by lack of market demand and perhaps mispricing or insufficient marketing by the enterprise. To prevent this, contingency plans (like seeking additional grants, diversifying services, or scaling operations to demand) are needed. Essentially, the enterprise and its customers/partners need to find the right balance to keep the venture economically sound to avoid a collapse that would undo the gains.

-   

-   

    **Dependency and Maintenance Issues:** The restoration approach might inadvertently create a **dependency on continuous human intervention**. If the ecosystem comes to rely on regular stocking (instead of natural recruitment), any interruption (due to funding gaps or technical failures) could leave the ecosystem in a lurch, potentially worse off if natural reproduction was not re-established. This risk means the value created is fragile unless the project plans an exit or handover strategy where nature can sustain itself or local entities can continue the work. Likewise, the sophisticated equipment (pumps, alarms) carries risk: a prolonged power outage or mechanical failure could cause a mass die-off in the hatchery tanks, destroying the fish (value loss to project and nature). Redundancies like backup power and alarms (which exist) are in place to minimize this risk, but it remains an area of vigilance.

-   

By anticipating these co-destructions, the Dawetrest team works to minimize them through careful management and stakeholder engagement. The aim is to ensure that the project’s footprint remains net-positive, swiftly correcting any negative side-effects that emerge.

## Partnerships

The success of the Green Hatchery is underpinned by a strong network of **partnerships**. These partnerships bring complementary resources, knowledge, and legitimacy. Key existing and potential partners include:

-   

-   

    **Academic & Research Partners:** The partnership with the **University of Zagreb (FSB)** is crucial[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}. FSB provides engineering and scientific expertise for designing the hatchery system (e.g. water recirculation technology, monitoring equipment). They also help with data analysis and publish results, giving the project scientific credibility. Additional research partners could include biology departments (for fish health and ecology) and institutes like the **Ruđer Bošković Institute** (if water quality analysis is needed). Such partners ensure the project is grounded in sound science and can innovate.

-   

-   

    **Local NGOs and Community Organizations:** As noted, **fisheries and angling clubs** (e.g. ŠRU Odra, and Osijek-Baranja fishing associations) are active partners[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}. They contribute manpower for releases and serve as liaisons to the local fishing community. **Conservation NGOs** like regional wildlife organizations or BirdLife partners can join to assist with bird monitoring and habitat improvements. For example, a bird-watching club might partner to create observation hides and conduct bird counts. **Community associations** (like a local eco-group or cultural association) can partner on events, ensuring the broader public is engaged.

-   

-   

    **Government and Public Sector:** The **Municipality of Draž** is a key partner, possibly providing logistical support (access roads, utilities to the site) and integrating the project into local development plans. **Osijek-Baranja County** and **Hrvatske Vode** (water authority) partner by aligning the hatchery with regional water management and environmental strategies, potentially even providing technical support for the side-arm restoration. The **Kopački Rit Nature Park Authority** is a partner in coordinating conservation goals – they might partner to ensure that hatchery efforts complement the park’s management (e.g., avoiding species that might become invasive in the park, co-promoting eco-tourism in the region). On a higher level, the project is part of the **EU Mission “Restore our Waters”** network, essentially partnering with the European Commission and Mission Board. This partnership offers funding and a platform to share outcomes across Europe, as well as policy support.

-   

-   

    **Private Sector and Suppliers:** The hatchery relies on specialized suppliers for equipment and feed. For instance, a company providing **water pumps and aerators** can be viewed as a partner if they offer training, maintenance support, or discounted efficient models (perhaps as part of their corporate social responsibility). There might be partnership potential with a **renewable energy provider** – for example, a solar panel company could partner to install solar cells at the site, powering the facility in exchange for publicity as a green energy champion. Local agricultural producers could partner by supplying environmentally friendly fish feed (e.g., locally grown corn or insect-based protein feed) – a partnership that could reduce costs and carbon footprint.

-   

-   

    **Tourism and Educational Partners:** The success of eco-tourism services will depend on partnerships with the **tourism sector**. Local tour operators, travel agencies, or even international eco-tourism networks (like Birdlife’s travel arm or fishing tour companies) can partner to include the hatchery in their itineraries. A partnership with **nearby accommodations** (rural bed-and-breakfasts, campgrounds) can create packages for visitors (e.g., a weekend “Fish and Birds of the Danube” package). On the educational side, partnerships with **schools and universities** ensure a steady stream of educational visits; e.g., a memorandum of understanding with the local school district for annual field trips, or with the University of Osijek’s biology program for internships at the hatchery.

-   

-   

    **Replication and Network Partners:** In aiming to replicate the model, the hatchery engages partners in other regions. Under the DaWetRest project, **associated regions** and sister sites are partners who learn from and possibly share resources with the Draž hatchery. For example, a partner site in Hungary or Serbia might exchange fingerlings or coordinate release strategies for migratory fish. Global networks like the **Freshwater Life Network** or **Ramsar Wetland City initiative** could become partners for knowledge exchange, giving the hatchery more visibility and input from similar projects worldwide.

-   

Each partnership is governed by mutual benefit: the hatchery gains support, expertise, or reach; partners gain results aligned with their interests (be it research outputs, conservation outcomes, or business opportunities). Building a diverse partnership web also anchors the project firmly in its socio-economic context, making it resilient. Future governance might formalize some of these partnerships (as described next) to ensure they persist beyond the initial EU project timeline.

## Governance

The **governance** structure of the Dawetrest Green Hatchery defines how decisions are made, who holds influence, and how accountability is maintained. Given the multi-stakeholder nature of the project, governance is designed to be **inclusive, transparent, and adaptive**. Key features and suggestions for governance include:

-   

-   

    **Multi-Stakeholder Steering Committee:** The project operates under the umbrella of the DaWetRest consortium during the funded period, which provides a form of governance (with work package leaders, periodic consortium meetings, etc.). Locally, a **steering committee** or management board is in place (or proposed) that includes representatives from major stakeholder groups: project leaders (FSB/innovation center), the Municipality of Draž, local fisheries NGO leaders, and possibly a Nature Park or Hrvatske Vode representative. Including a broad set of voices ensures that decisions (like how many fish to release, or how to balance tourism with conservation) reflect diverse interests. It also enhances legitimacy—community members see their peers in governance roles.

-   

-   

    **Transparent Decision-Making:** Governance processes are kept transparent through regular public reporting and meetings. For example, the hatchery management could present an **annual report** to the community and partners, detailing accomplishments, financial status, ecological impacts (fish survival rates, bird counts), and next year’s plan. Public Q&A sessions or open days allow stakeholders to query and understand decisions. This transparency builds trust and makes it easier to handle any controversies (e.g., if a certain practice isn’t working and needs change, stakeholders are brought into the loop early).

-   

-   

    **Adaptive Management:** The governance approach is flexible, following **adaptive management principles** common in conservation. The team sets objectives and monitors results (e.g., track water quality, fish growth, bird populations). If outcomes deviate from targets, the governance group can decide on course corrections—perhaps adjusting the hatchery production, modifying release timing, or changing tourism practices. This iterative decision-making is science-informed: advisors (scientists from FSB or ecologists) provide input to the governance board so that policies can change based on evidence. For instance, if data show a fish species struggling, governance might decide to suspend releases of that species and focus on habitat factors first.

-   

-   

    **Roles and Responsibility Sharing:** Clear definition of roles is part of governance. The hatchery likely has an **operational manager** (day-to-day in charge, perhaps employed by one of the partners or the municipality) responsible for implementing the plan. The steering committee provides oversight and strategic guidance rather than micromanaging. Partners have defined responsibilities: e.g., the local NGO might oversee organizing volunteers, the municipality handles site maintenance like road access or utilities, the university partner oversees scientific monitoring. By formalizing these roles (potentially through MOUs or agreements), the governance ensures accountability. Everyone knows who is responsible for what, and if something goes amiss (say, a pump fails), the governance protocols dictate how decisions are made to address it (the manager can act within a mandate or escalate to the committee for big expenses).

-   

-   

    **Financial Governance and Sustainability:** A crucial aspect is how revenues and costs are managed. The governance structure likely includes a financial officer or treasurer (perhaps from the municipality or NGO) who manages the budget and ensures transparency in spending grant funds and any tourism income. Plans for sustainability—like creating a **small trust fund or revolving fund** from tourism revenue to keep the hatchery running post-grant—should be governed collectively. For example, governance might decide that a portion of any income from tours or permits goes into an earmarked maintenance fund. If larger capital is needed (for equipment replacement in a few years), the governance board would collectively seek additional funding (writing grant proposals or soliciting sponsors), rather than leaving it to one entity.

-   

-   

    **Legal Form and Long-Term Governance:** While currently a project, for longevity the initiative might formalize into a legal entity. One suggestion is to establish a **local cooperative or nonprofit organization** to run the Green Hatchery after the EU project. Such an entity could have membership from various stakeholder groups, effectively institutionalizing the multi-stakeholder governance beyond the initial funding period. This structure would allow it to enter partnerships, apply for grants, charge for services, and manage property in a stable way. Ensuring that governance survives leadership changes (by training local successors and embedding governance in an institution) is key to replicability and long-term impact.

-   

In summary, good governance for the Green Hatchery means **shared power, evidence-based decisions, and clear accountability**. This not only helps avoid conflicts and missteps but also models a form of collaborative leadership that can be emulated in similar projects elsewhere.

## Resources

*Key Resources:* *View of the Green Hatchery facility in Draž, showing the core physical resources – a modern hatchery building and circular fish rearing tanks – integrated into the natural surroundings. Robust infrastructure (tanks, pumps, aerators) and natural assets (water from the Dunavac) form the foundation of the project’s resources.*

The **resources** block covers all the assets required for the hatchery to function – physical, natural, human, financial, and informational. The Dawetrest Green Hatchery draws on a blend of built infrastructure and ecosystem resources:

-   

-   

    **Physical Infrastructure:** The project has established a **state-of-the-art hatchery facility**[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources"}. This includes several circular rearing **tanks** (as seen in the image above) for holding and growing fish. Each tank is outfitted with aeration diffusers and water recirculation pipes. High-efficiency **water pumps** circulate water through filters, maintaining quality and oxygen levels for the fish. An array of **blowers and aerators** supplies oxygen to the water continuously. A backup **generator** or battery system is in place to ensure pumps run during power outages, and a **GSM alarm system** sends alerts to staff if any critical parameter (like oxygen level or pump function) falls out of range. The hatchery building itself houses an office/lab space for monitoring water chemistry, a storage area for feed and equipment, and possibly a small incubation room for fish eggs. The site is secured by **fencing** to protect against predators (like herons helping themselves to fish in the tanks) and to ensure visitor safety. Additionally, specialized **fish transport containers** (tanks with aeration used on a trailer or pickup truck) are a critical resource for moving fish to release sites. This robust physical setup, partly achieved by **repurposing existing facilities**[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources"} (possibly an old fish farm or unused ponds adapted into the new system), allows the project to reliably rear large quantities of fish.

-   

-   

    **Natural Resources:** The hatchery relies on several **biophysical stocks** (detailed more in the next section) as inputs. Key among them is **water** – clean water likely drawn from the Topoljski Dunavac or a connected groundwater source to fill and maintain the tanks. The project leverages the natural water temperature and chemistry of the local environment, possibly doing minimal heating or treatment (using the “existing natural potentials” of the site[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources"}). **Broodstock fish** (adult specimens of native species) are a vital living resource; these either came from local wild populations or from partner hatcheries and are used to spawn the next generation. The surrounding land provides space and some ecosystem services (e.g., soil and gravel for natural filtration systems, if any constructed wetlands are used to treat effluent). Even the climate (sunlight and ambient temperature) is a resource that influences growth rates. The project also consumes **fish feed**, which is derived from natural resources (commercial feed typically contains fish meal, grains, etc.). Ensuring feed is sustainably sourced (perhaps using more plant-based or insect-based protein to reduce pressure on wild fish stocks) is an important consideration in resource use.

-   

-   

    **Human Resources:** Knowledgeable and dedicated **people** are one of the most critical resources. The hatchery has a small team of trained staff – possibly an aquaculture specialist managing daily operations, a technician or caretaker maintaining equipment, and a part-time biologist or vet checking fish health. Volunteers from local fishing clubs and students from the university are additional human resources that bolster capacity during peak activities (like mass release days or community events). The project also relies on **expert consultants** at times (engineers from FSB who help calibrate the systems, or ecologists who design monitoring protocols). The social capital and passion these individuals bring are intangible resources that drive the project’s quality.

-   

-   

    **Financial Resources:** The initial funding through the **EU Horizon/DaWetRest grant** provided the capital for construction and the first years of operation[[cordis.europa.eu]{.underline}](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101113015/results#:~:text=Total%20cost){alt="https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101113015/results#:~:text=Total%20cost"}[[cordis.europa.eu]{.underline}](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101113015/results#:~:text=Amount%20of%20money%2C%20by%20way,equal%20to%20the%20grant%20amount){alt="https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101113015/results#:~:text=Amount%20of%20money%2C%20by%20way,equal%20to%20the%20grant%20amount"}. This grant (part of an ≈€9 million project budget across all sites) covered equipment purchase and setup. Ongoing financial resources include portions of that grant allocated to operational costs, as well as any **supplementary funding** from local or national bodies (e.g., the Croatian government or county might contribute small funds or in-kind support). As the project develops, **revenue from tourism or services** becomes a resource – money from fishing permits, guided tour fees, or donations can be re-invested in the hatchery. Additionally, the project could access new grants (for example, environment or rural development funds) to expand or continue its work. Maintaining a diverse base of financial resources (grant, earned income, sponsorship) will be key for resilience.

-   

-   

    **Information and Digital Resources:** Lastly, the project benefits from various informational tools – a **monitoring database** where water quality data, growth rates, and wildlife observations are recorded (potentially a cloud-based platform accessible to partners). It may utilize a **GSM-based monitoring system** that not only alarms but logs data from sensors (temperature, oxygen, pH) in real-time. This data is a resource for making decisions and demonstrating impact. The project also has communication materials (website, brochures, signage) which are resources that help in outreach and education.

-   

Collectively, these resources — infrastructure, nature, people, funds, and information — form the backbone of the enterprise. The innovative aspect of the Green Hatchery is how it combines them: using **sustainable natural resource use and existing facilities** to minimize environmental footprint while maximizing output[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Alongside%20restoration%20works%20aimed%20at,sustainable%20use%20of%20natural%20resources"}, and using community human resources to extend what financial resources can do. Proper management of these resources ensures the project’s operations are efficient and effective.

## Biophysical Stocks

The **biophysical stocks** are the natural capital inputs and stocks in the environment that the hatchery draws upon or affects. In the context of this project, important biophysical stocks include:

-   

-   

    **Water Resources:** The Topoljski Dunavac and connected Danube waters are a fundamental stock. The hatchery uses water from the wetland – either directly pumped in or via a well that taps into the same aquifer – as the medium for fish rearing. This water stock provides the natural temperature regime and biochemical environment suited for native species. It’s crucial that this water remains clean and abundant. The project’s use of water is likely non-consumptive (returned after use), but evaporation and minor consumption occur. Maintaining the quantity and quality of this water stock (through careful monitoring and avoiding pollution) is key to project success and also a responsibility, since this stock also supports all wild aquatic life.

-   

-   

    **Fish (Breeding Stock):** The living genetic stock of **native fish** is another biophysical stock. The project initially needed a source of broodstock (adult fish) for species like carp, tench, etc. Some of these may have been taken from wild populations in the Danube floodplain (with permits) or borrowed from existing hatcheries that had pure strains. These parent fish represent the genetic reservoir that will produce all hatchery offspring. It’s critical to manage this stock by keeping them healthy and perhaps occasionally introducing new wild individuals to avoid genetic bottlenecks. The wild populations of these fish in the Danube system are also stocks that the project aims to augment – the hatchery essentially “invests” fish into the wild stock, growing the overall population capital in nature.

-   

-   

    **Land and Soil:** The physical land on which the facility sits is a stock of natural capital. The site likely occupies a small area that may have been a former pond or riverside land. The soil and geological conditions matter; for instance, the permeability of soil affects if ponds can hold water or how drainage is handled. In a broader sense, the entire floodplain’s land is a stock that provides space for wetlands to exist. By ensuring no heavy contamination or permanent damage to land (e.g., avoiding chemicals that could accumulate in soil), the project protects this stock. When the side-arm (Dunavac) was restored (dredged or reconnected), that action modified the land/water interface, which is part of renewing the natural capital of land and hydrology.

-   

-   

    **Wildlife Populations:** The **bird populations** and other wildlife can be seen as stocks in the environment. The herons, storks, and others have baseline population levels that the project hopes to increase by providing more food (fish). These animal populations are regenerative stocks – given more resources, they can produce more offspring and grow. Monitoring their numbers is like tracking a natural capital index; if the stock of birds increases, it indicates success. Conversely, any decline might signal an issue in the ecosystem.

-   

-   

    **Nutrient and Energy Stocks:** On a different note, consider the **nutrient stock** in the ecosystem. The hatchery adds fish (biomass) into the water; those fish represent nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) that eventually become part of the food web. If fish get eaten by birds, those nutrients might go into bird guano and vegetation, cycling through the ecosystem. This is a positive augmentation of the natural nutrient stocks in a controlled way. However, overfeeding fish in the hatchery could lead to nutrient waste (uneaten feed) which if released could cause eutrophication; thus, feed input is managed to not exceed what the system can assimilate. Additionally, the **energy stock** – often overlooked – is relevant: the project consumes electricity (which in Croatia’s grid is partly from fossil fuels, partly renewable). This draws on national energy stocks. If solar panels are installed in future, the project would draw on the stock of sunlight – a renewable stock – to run operations, reducing draw on non-renewable energy stocks.

-   

-   

    **Materials and Consumables:** The construction and operation used materials that come from natural stocks: e.g., **construction materials** (sand, gravel, cement, metal for tanks) come from quarries and mines; **plastic** piping and tank materials come from petroleum stock; fuel for transport draws on oil stocks. While these are mostly one-time inputs, they constitute an environmental footprint. The ongoing use of fish feed ties to agricultural stocks (soy, grain) or ocean fish stocks (for fishmeal) if used. The project likely selected feed that is formulated to be sustainable, but it’s worth noting that each kilogram of feed has its own chain of natural stocks. Minimizing waste and choosing sustainable suppliers helps ensure the project’s demand doesn’t deplete distant stocks unsustainably.

-   

By acknowledging these biophysical stocks, the hatchery can manage its resource use responsibly. For example, recycling water internally reduces draw from the river; sourcing feed from sustainable operations helps global fish stocks; and improving the local fish and bird stocks adds to the region’s natural capital. The Flourishing Business Canvas approach ensures that increasing one stock (fish) is not done at the unintended expense of another (water quality, etc.), striving for a net gain in *total* natural capital.

## Activities

The **activities** block enumerates the core actions the hatchery enterprise undertakes to deliver its value and achieve its goals. The Dawetrest Green Hatchery’s key activities include:

-   

-   

    **Fish Breeding and Rearing:** This is the primary operational activity. It involves selecting and maintaining **broodstock fish**, inducing spawning (e.g. via environmental cues or hormone treatments if needed for some species), and caring for eggs and larvae. Hatchery staff monitor incubation tanks until eggs hatch, then transfer fry to rearing tanks or ponds. Daily tasks include feeding the juvenile fish a balanced diet, grading them by size to reduce competition, and monitoring growth. Maintaining optimal water quality is part of this activity – staff check temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, and ammonia levels frequently, adjusting aeration or water flow as needed. This also includes treating any fish health issues (isolating sick fish, applying salt baths or other remedies). The activity is year-round, though certain seasons are critical (spring and early summer are typical spawning times for cyprinids).

-   

-   

    **Fish Release Operations:** At scheduled times (twice a year, typically spring and fall), the hatchery conducts **stocking events** to release fish into the wild. Preparations include conditioning the fish (ensuring they are healthy and of sufficient size to survive in the wild), then carefully netting and transferring them into aerated transport tanks. The team coordinates with local NGOs and authorities on timing and locations – for instance, choosing a day when water levels are suitable and predators won’t immediately overwhelm the released fish. During each event, hundreds of kilograms of fish are released (approximately 600 kg per event to total \~1,200 kg/year). This activity is both technical and public-facing: it often serves as a media or community event, so staff and volunteers might also engage in explaining the process to observers or involving local children in a symbolic release of a few fish. Post-release, there is an activity of monitoring – checking on the dispersal and survival of released fish via nets or electrofishing surveys, which informs future release strategies.

-   

-   

    **Facility and Equipment Maintenance:** Running a hatchery means constant **maintenance activities** to ensure reliability. Daily, staff clean the tanks (remove waste, change or flush water if it’s a flow-through system, clean biofilters if recirculating). They inspect pumps, aerators, and sensor equipment for proper function. Preventative maintenance like replacing pump impellers or cleaning aeration stones is scheduled regularly. The backup systems (generator fuel, battery charge, alarm functionality) are tested. Any infrastructure issues (a tear in a tank liner, a pipe leak) are promptly repaired. These maintenance tasks prevent failures that could cause fish losses.

-   

-   

    **Environmental Monitoring:** The project carries out continuous **monitoring of environmental indicators** as part of its adaptive management. Activities include water quality testing in the Dunavac (measuring parameters like oxygen, nutrients, perhaps pollutant levels pre- and post-intervention), and **biomonitoring** of wildlife. For example, staff or partners conduct **bird surveys** at intervals to count species and numbers of wetland birds utilizing the area (checking if there’s an uptick in fish-eating bird populations). They may also monitor aquatic vegetation and invertebrates as indicators of ecosystem health. Soil or sediment samples might be taken yearly to ensure no accumulation of any contaminants from hatchery effluent. These monitoring activities are often done in collaboration with experts or citizen scientists and feed into evaluation reports.

-   

-   

    **Data Analysis and Reporting:** Tied to monitoring is the activity of **analyzing data and reporting** findings. Project team members compile growth rates of fish, survival percentages, and ecological monitoring results to evaluate if targets are met. They prepare technical reports (for the EU funders, for local authorities, for scientific purposes) that document outcomes like “X number of fish released, Y% survival after 3 months” or “bird counts increased by Z% over 2 years”. This analytical activity is crucial for demonstrating impact and learning from the results. It also involves adjusting internal protocols (e.g., if analysis shows one species had poor post-release survival, they might alter the size at release or season).

-   

-   

    **Community and Educational Events:** The hatchery team actively engages in **outreach activities**. They organize or participate in events such as World Wetlands Day celebrations, local fairs, or school visits. During these events, they might give presentations, showcase live specimens or visual displays, and lead tours of the facility.
