There may be periodic volunteer activities like “wetland cleanup day” or tree planting along the riverbank, which are organized by the project to involve the community. Education-focused activities include hosting interns or trainees, and possibly developing educational materials (posters, a small booklet on Baranja wetlands) as part of their tasks.

-   

-   

    **Marketing and Networking:** Ensuring the project’s sustainability requires spreading the word, so marketing is an activity – updating social media with success stories or beautiful nature photos, maintaining a webpage, and engaging journalists for coverage. Networking with other similar initiatives (attending conferences, exchange visits with other hatchery projects) is another activity that keeps the project at the cutting edge and opens doors for future cooperation.

-   

-   

    **Governance and Administration:** Internally, there are governance activities – meetings of the steering committee, administrative tasks like budgeting, procurement of supplies (feed, fuel, parts), and ensuring regulatory compliance (filing permit renewals, etc.). These behind-the-scenes activities keep the organizational aspect running smoothly.

-   

All these activities are carefully choreographed to deliver on the mission. By managing them effectively, the hatchery is able to produce healthy fish, integrate them into the environment, engage people, and adapt based on feedback – the essence of a flourishing, learning enterprise.

## Ecosystem Services

**Ecosystem services** are the benefits that people and other organisms obtain from ecosystems. The Green Hatchery both relies on certain ecosystem services and enhances others through its operations. Key ecosystem services associated with this initiative include:

-   

-   

    **Habitat Provision (Supporting Service):** The project enhances the **habitat for aquatic and wetland species**. By restocking native fish and improving water conditions, it contributes to the ecosystem’s ability to support a rich community of life. The floodplain water body (Topoljski Dunavac) can be seen as providing the service of *habitat provisioning* – it offers spawning and feeding grounds for fish, and feeding and nesting areas for birds. The hatchery’s work increases the quality of this service by boosting biodiversity and complexity in the food web. Indirectly, healthier fish populations can lead to more robust aquatic plant growth (through grazing control or nutrient cycling), further improving habitat structure. This service benefits not just wildlife but also people who value a thriving natural environment.

-   

-   

    **Food Provision (Provisioning Service):** Historically, wetlands like these provide food in the form of fish and other aquatic resources to local communities. The hatchery explicitly augments the **provisioning service of fish**. While the released fish are not immediately meant for human harvest, over time a sustainable fishery could be an outcome – local anglers may catch some of these native fish for consumption or recreation under regulated conditions. In a broader sense, the fish also serve as “food” for predatory wildlife (herons, etc.), so the project is enhancing the provisioning service that the ecosystem offers to those animals. Should the community decide in future to allow limited artisanal fishing once populations are stable, the hatchery will have directly contributed to the ecosystem’s provisioning service in a sustainable way (unlike commercial overfishing, this would be a replenished yield).

-   

-   

    **Water Quality Regulation (Regulating Service):** Wetland ecosystems naturally perform **water purification** by cycling nutrients and trapping sediments. A healthy fish community can contribute to this regulating service. For example, benthivorous fish (those that stir the sediment) can help control excess nutrient build-up, and predatory fish can prevent algal blooms by consuming zooplankton predators. The hatchery’s effect of improving the ecological balance may enhance the wetland’s ability to regulate water quality – leading to clearer water with balanced algae levels. Additionally, if the project restored flow in the side-arm, that action rejuvenates the wetland’s filtering capacity (fresh water flowing through wetlands can be cleaned of pollutants). This service benefits humans by maintaining cleaner water entering downstream ecosystems or even seeping into groundwater.

-   

-   

    **Climate Regulation and Flood Mitigation (Regulating Services):** By restoring wetland function, the project indirectly supports **climate regulation** and **flood control** services. Wetlands are known carbon sinks; healthier wetland vegetation and soils can sequester carbon, albeit modestly in this case. The presence of a connected floodplain water body provides space for floodwaters during high Danube levels, thereby protecting surrounding areas – this flood mitigation capacity is an ecosystem service of floodplains. The hatchery itself doesn’t manage floods, but as part of the larger restoration (with side-arm reconnection), it contributes to reactivating the natural flood buffering service. This can reduce potential flood damage costs for local communities and agriculture by giving floodwaters a place to expand.

-   

-   

    **Recreation and Ecotourism (Cultural Service):** A flourishing ecosystem offers tremendous **recreational value**. The project directly boosts the **cultural ecosystem service** of nature recreation. Birdwatching, fishing, photography, and nature hiking are all recreational services supplied by a vibrant wetland. With more birds and fish to see, and via the trails or tours the project provides, people derive enjoyment, inspiration, and even spiritual value from the ecosystem. The scenic beauty of the Baranja wetlands is preserved and enhanced, which is a non-material benefit humans greatly appreciate. As evidence of this service, one can point to visitors spending leisure time and money to experience the area – a sign that the cultural service is tangible and valued.

-   

-   

    **Educational and Scientific Value (Cultural/Supporting Service):** The wetland and the project serve as a living laboratory, which is an **educational ecosystem service**. The knowledge gained and transmitted because of the healthy ecosystem is a valuable service to society. This includes traditional knowledge (fishermen learning about sustainable practices tied to the ecosystem’s rhythms) and formal scientific research opportunities. It’s somewhat abstract, but many frameworks consider the knowledge and educational opportunities from nature as part of cultural services. In this case, the project has explicitly created an educational benefit stream by having an ecosystem in recovery that can be studied and learned from, locally and for replicability across Europe[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Zajedno%20%C4%87emo%20demonstrirati%20izvedivost%2C%20ponovljivost,obnovi%20i%20o%C4%8Duvanju%20mo%C4%8Dvarnih%20ekosustava){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=Zajedno%20%C4%87emo%20demonstrirati%20izvedivost%2C%20ponovljivost,obnovi%20i%20o%C4%8Duvanju%20mo%C4%8Dvarnih%20ekosustava"}.

-   

By both utilizing and enhancing these ecosystem services, the Green Hatchery ensures that human-nature interactions are positive and reinforcing. For instance, it takes the service of clean water for fish culture and returns even cleaner water to nature; it uses the habitat service of the floodplain and amplifies it by adding more life. These improvements in ecosystem services demonstrate the broader impact of the project – not just on immediate stakeholders, but on **everyone who benefits from a well-functioning Danube floodplain**, from local communities to global society.

In conclusion, the Dawetrest Green Hatchery is much more than a fish breeding facility – it is a holistic enterprise that **interweaves ecological restoration with community development**. Through its 17 business model dimensions, we see a complex yet coherent picture: **stakeholders** ranging from fish to farmers are engaged; their **needs** are addressed via creative **value propositions** (fish stocking, eco-tourism, education); critical **activities and resources** are marshaled with an eye on sustainability; and the **value created** is shared broadly, while potential harms are carefully managed. Partnerships and good governance bind these elements together, ensuring the initiative remains adaptive and resilient. This flourishing business canvas not only guides the current project in Draž, but also offers a blueprint for how similar **nature-based enterprises** can be designed elsewhere – ultimately fulfilling the goal of replicability and scaling impact for healthier wetlands and communities well into the future.[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20activities,ecosystems%20along%20the%20Danube%20River"}[[voda.hr]{.underline}](https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae){alt="https://www.voda.hr/hr/projekt/dawetrest#:~:text=In%20collaboration%20with%20local%20fisheries,families%20Ardeidae%2C%20Ciconiidae%2C%20and%20Threskiornithidae"}
